summary: How somites, lateral plate mesoderm, and the pharyngeal arches build the bones, muscles, and joints, and how limb buds grow, rotate, and ossify. Exam questions link an embryonic step to its adult nerve supply, curve, or birth defect.

points: Paraxial mesoderm segments into somites from about day 20 (week 3 to 5).
Sclerotome (ventromedial) surrounds the notochord and neural tube to form vertebrae and ribs.
Dermomyotome splits into dermatome (dermis of the back) and myotome (skeletal muscle).
Epaxial myotome forms the deep back muscles (erector spinae), supplied by dorsal rami.
Hypaxial myotome forms limb and body wall muscles, supplied by ventral rami.
Each segment keeps its own spinal nerve, which is the basis of dermatomes and myotomes.
Resegmentation: each vertebral body forms from the caudal half of one sclerotome fused to the cranial half of the next.
Because of this shift, segmental arteries end up running across the middle of each vertebral body.
The spinal nerve exits at the level of the disc, and each myotome bridges two vertebrae so muscles can move the spine.
Notochord persists between bodies as the nucleus pulposus; the annulus fibrosus forms from sclerotome cells.
A notochord remnant can give rise to a chordoma (often sacral or clival).
Limb buds appear in week 4 (upper about day 24, lower about day 28): lateral plate mesoderm core covered by ectoderm.
Limb muscle comes from hypaxial myotome cells that migrate into the bud; limb bone, cartilage, and tendon come from lateral plate mesoderm.
Apical ectodermal ridge (AER) secretes FGFs that drive proximal to distal outgrowth; loss of AER gives limb truncation.
Zone of polarizing activity (ZPA) at the posterior bud secretes sonic hedgehog for anterior to posterior (thumb to little finger) pattern.
Extra Shh activity on the anterior side gives mirror digits and preaxial polydactyly.
HOX genes set the identity of each segment; HOXD13 mutation causes synpolydactyly.
Thalidomide during limb bud formation (about days 24 to 36 after fertilization) causes phocomelia, with hands or feet attached close to the trunk.
In week 7 to 8 the upper limb rotates 90 degrees laterally and the lower limb rotates about 90 degrees medially.
Upper limb: extensors end up posterior and the thumb lateral.
Lower limb: extensors end up anterior, flexors posterior, and the big toe medial.
Medial rotation twists lower limb dermatomes into a spiral (L4 medial leg, L5 dorsum of foot, S1 lateral foot).
Intramembranous: mesenchyme turns straight into bone (skull vault, facial bones, most of the clavicle).
Endochondral: a hyaline cartilage model is replaced by bone (long bones, vertebrae, skull base).
Primary ossification centers appear in the diaphysis of most long bones by about week 12; secondary centers form in the epiphyses, mostly after birth.
Clavicle is the first bone to start ossifying (about week 5 to 6).
Joints form from interzone mesenchyme between bone models; synovial joints form when the interzone cavitates into a joint cavity.

tricks.label: Epaxial goes to the back door
tricks.text: Epaxial muscles sit behind the vertebral axis and are reached by the dorsal ramus. Everything in front (limbs, body wall) is hypaxial and comes off the ventral ramus.

tricks.label: Count the arches by nerve
tricks.text: Arches 1, 2, 3 go with cranial nerves 5, 7, 9 (skip one each time). Arches 4 and 6 both use CN X: superior laryngeal for 4, recurrent laryngeal for 6.

tricks.label: Thumbs out, big toes in
tricks.text: Upper limb turns out (lateral) and lower limb turns in (medial). That is why the thumb is lateral, the big toe is medial, and the knee faces forward while the elbow faces back.

highYield: Erector spinae are epaxial and supplied by dorsal rami; limb muscles are hypaxial and supplied by ventral rami.
Nucleus pulposus is the notochord remnant; chordoma arises from notochord rests.
AER makes FGF for length; ZPA makes Shh for thumb to pinky order.
Ectopic anterior Shh expression causes polydactyly.
Thalidomide exposure during limb bud formation causes phocomelia.
Skull vault and most of the clavicle form by intramembranous ossification; long bones form by endochondral ossification.
First arch muscles chew (CN V3); second arch muscles make facial expression (CN VII).
Medial rotation of the lower limb puts the knee extensors in front and twists the dermatomes into a spiral.
pitfalls: Dermatome in a somite means the embryonic block that forms dermis; in the clinic it means a skin area supplied by one spinal nerve.
Limb muscles come from somites (myotome), while limb bones and tendons come from lateral plate mesoderm.
The vertebral body is built from two neighboring sclerotome halves, so it does not match a single somite.
Stylopharyngeus is the only third arch muscle (CN IX) and is not a constrictor; the pharyngeal constrictors are fourth arch muscles (CN X).

dumps.p: Draw a cross section of a week 4 embryo showing the neural tube, notochord, and one somite. Label sclerotome, dermatome, and myotome, then draw arrows to what each becomes and which ramus supplies the muscles.
l: Somite comes from paraxial mesoderm
Sclerotome moves around notochord and neural tube to form vertebrae and ribs
Dermatome forms dermis of the back
Epaxial myotome forms deep back muscles supplied by dorsal rami
Hypaxial myotome forms limb and body wall muscles supplied by ventral rami
Notochord becomes the nucleus pulposus
Vertebral body forms from caudal half of one sclerotome plus cranial half of the next

dumps.p: Draw a limb bud and label the AER, the ZPA, and the dorsal ectoderm. Beside each, write its signal molecule, the axis it controls, and the defect you see when it goes wrong.
l: AER at the distal tip secretes FGF
AER drives proximal to distal growth; loss gives truncation
ZPA at the posterior margin secretes sonic hedgehog
Shh sets anterior to posterior digit order; ectopic anterior Shh gives polydactyly
Dorsal ectoderm WNT7 sets dorsal to ventral pattern
HOX genes set segment identity
Thalidomide during limb bud formation causes phocomelia
Upper limb rotates laterally, lower limb medially in weeks 7 to 8

summary: The microscopic structure of the three muscle types, compact and spongy bone, the bone cells, the growth plate, and the three joint classes. Exam questions ask you to predict what changes in a sarcomere, a growth plate, or a joint when something goes wrong.

points: Sarcomere runs from one Z line to the next; thin (actin) filaments anchor at the Z line.
A band is the full length of the thick (myosin) filaments; it stays the same length during contraction.
I band holds thin filaments only and shortens.
H zone holds thick filaments only and shortens; the M line sits in its center and links thick filaments.
Z lines move closer together because filaments slide past each other; no filament changes length.
Skeletal: long multinucleate fibers with peripheral nuclei, striated, triads (T tubule plus two terminal cisternae) at the A to I junction.
Skeletal regeneration comes from satellite cells.
Cardiac: branched cells with one or two central nuclei, striated, dyads at the Z line.
Intercalated discs join cardiac cells: gap junctions for electrical spread, desmosomes and fascia adherens for mechanical strength.
Smooth: fusiform cells with one central nucleus, no striations, dense bodies anchor actin (Z line equivalent).
Smooth muscle uses caveolae instead of a T tubule system and can divide (hyperplasia).
Compact bone is built of osteons: concentric lamellae around a central (Haversian) canal with vessels and nerves.
Volkmann canals run across the bone and connect Haversian canals to each other and to the periosteum.
Osteocytes sit in lacunae and touch each other through canaliculi joined by gap junctions.
Spongy (cancellous) bone is a lattice of trabeculae with marrow in the spaces; no osteons.
Woven bone has random collagen and is weak (fetal bone, fracture callus, Paget disease); lamellar bone has organized layers and replaces it.
Osteoblasts come from mesenchymal stem cells (RUNX2) and secrete type I collagen osteoid and alkaline phosphatase.
Osteoblasts express RANKL and OPG, so they control osteoclast activity; PTH receptors are on osteoblasts.
Osteocytes are osteoblasts trapped in matrix; they sense load and secrete FGF23 (phosphate loss in urine) and sclerostin.
Osteoclasts come from the monocyte and macrophage line, fuse into multinucleated cells, and need M-CSF and RANKL.
Osteoclast ruffled border pumps acid (H+ made by carbonic anhydrase II) and releases cathepsin K into Howship lacunae.
Zones from epiphysis to diaphysis: reserve, proliferative, hypertrophic, calcification, ossification.
Achondroplasia: activating FGFR3 mutation slows chondrocyte proliferation, giving a thin proliferative zone and short long bones.
Rickets: poor mineralization lets the hypertrophic zone pile up, giving a wide, irregular plate with frayed, cupped metaphyses.
Fibrous joints: sutures, syndesmoses (distal tibiofibular), gomphoses (tooth in socket).
Cartilaginous joints: synchondroses use hyaline cartilage (growth plate, first sternocostal joint); symphyses use fibrocartilage (pubic symphysis, intervertebral disc).
Synovial joints: avascular articular hyaline cartilage with no perichondrium; synoviocytes make hyaluronan and lubricin for synovial fluid.

charts.title: Growth plate zones

Fails in rickets, leaving excess osteoid

tricks.label: HIZ shrinkage
tricks.text: During contraction the H zone, the I band, and the Z to Z distance (sarcomere) all shorten. The A band is the one that stays the same.

tricks.label: A is for Always
tricks.text: The A band is set by thick filament length, and myosin never changes length, so the A band always stays constant.

tricks.label: Blasts build, clasts cut
tricks.text: Osteoblasts build bone and come from mesenchyme. Osteoclasts cut bone and come from blood (monocytes), which is why they are multinucleated like other fused macrophages.

highYield: I band and H zone shorten during contraction; the A band stays constant.
Intercalated discs with gap junctions let cardiac muscle contract as a functional syncytium.
Osteoclasts are monocyte lineage cells that use cathepsin K and acid in Howship lacunae.
Osteocytes secrete FGF23, which increases urinary phosphate loss.
Achondroplasia (FGFR3 gain of function) shortens the proliferative zone, so endochondral bones are short while intramembranous bones grow normally.
Rickets widens the growth plate because hypertrophic cartilage is not mineralized and removed.
Articular cartilage has no blood supply and no perichondrium; it is fed by synovial fluid.
pitfalls: Triads belong to skeletal muscle; dyads belong to cardiac muscle.
Haversian canals run along the bone; Volkmann canals cross it.
Synchondroses are hyaline; symphyses are fibrocartilage.
Woven bone in an adult is abnormal (fracture callus, Paget disease, tumors); lamellar bone is the normal mature form.

dumps.p: Draw one sarcomere relaxed and the same sarcomere contracted. Label the Z lines, M line, A band, I band, and H zone in both, and mark which ones got shorter.
l: Sarcomere spans Z line to Z line
Thin actin filaments attach at Z lines
Thick myosin filaments are centered on the M line
A band equals thick filament length and stays constant
I band (thin only) shortens
H zone (thick only) shortens
Filaments slide; they do not change length

dumps.p: Draw a column of the epiphyseal growth plate from epiphysis to diaphysis and label the five zones. Next to it, show how the plate looks in achondroplasia and in rickets.
l: Reserve zone sits nearest the epiphysis
Proliferative zone has stacked dividing chondrocytes
Hypertrophic zone has large chondrocytes
Calcification zone mineralizes matrix
Ossification zone has osteoblasts laying bone on calcified cartilage
Achondroplasia: thin proliferative zone from FGFR3 activation
Rickets: wide, disorganized hypertrophic zone from failed mineralization

summary: The bones of the skull, spine, and limbs, the skull foramina and what passes through them, and the nerves that run against bone where fractures happen. Exam questions give a fracture or a curve and ask what structure or function is lost.

points: Cervical: transverse foramina carry the vertebral artery (usually C6 to C1); C3 to C6 have bifid spines; C7 is the vertebra prominens.
Atlas (C1) has no body and no spinous process; it holds the skull and allows nodding.
Axis (C2) has the dens, the pivot for head rotation at the atlantoaxial joint.
Thoracic: costal facets on bodies and transverse processes for ribs; long downward spines; ribs limit motion.
Lumbar: large kidney-shaped bodies for weight bearing; sagittal facets favor flexion and extension.
Thoracic and sacral kyphoses are primary curves present before birth.
Cervical lordosis appears with head control and lumbar lordosis with standing and walking (secondary curves).
Scoliosis is lateral curvature plus vertebral rotation; adolescent idiopathic scoliosis is most common in girls.
Excess kyphosis can follow osteoporotic compression fractures.
Severe thoracic scoliosis stiffens the chest wall, causing restrictive lung disease (low TLC and vital capacity, normal or high FEV1/FVC).
Superior orbital fissure: CN III, IV, V1, VI and the superior ophthalmic vein.
Foramen rotundum: V2. Foramen ovale: V3. Foramen spinosum: middle meningeal artery.
Internal acoustic meatus: CN VII and VIII. Jugular foramen: CN IX, X, XI and the internal jugular vein.
Foramen magnum: medulla, vertebral arteries, spinal roots of CN XI.
Pterion is where frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid bones meet; it is thin.
The anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery runs deep to the pterion, so a fracture there causes an epidural hematoma.
Clavicle fractures most often in the middle third.
Scapula: glenoid fossa for the humeral head, acromion and coracoid process for muscle and ligament attachment.
Radius is lateral (thumb side) and widest at the wrist; ulna is medial and widest at the elbow (olecranon).
Humeral surgical neck: axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery.
Midshaft humerus (radial groove): radial nerve and deep brachial artery.
Medial epicondyle: ulnar nerve. Supracondylar fracture: median nerve and brachial artery.
Scaphoid is the most fractured carpal (snuffbox tenderness); its blood enters distally, so the proximal pole can undergo avascular necrosis.
Lunate is the most dislocated carpal and can compress the median nerve.
Hip bone: ilium, ischium, and pubis meet and fuse at the acetabulum.
Femur carries body weight to the tibia; the fibula bears little weight but anchors muscles and forms the lateral malleolus.
Femoral neck fracture can tear the medial circumflex femoral artery and cause avascular necrosis of the femoral head.
Fibular neck fracture injures the common fibular nerve: foot drop, weak eversion, numb dorsum of foot.
Foot has medial longitudinal, lateral longitudinal, and transverse arches.
Medial longitudinal arch is held by the spring ligament, tibialis posterior tendon, and plantar aponeurosis; collapse gives flat foot (pes planus).

tricks.label: Standing Room Only
tricks.text: V1 passes through the Superior orbital fissure, V2 through foramen Rotundum, V3 through foramen Ovale.

tricks.label: So Long To Pinky, Here Comes The Thumb
tricks.text: Proximal row lateral to medial: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform. Distal row medial to lateral: hamate, capitate, trapezoid, trapezium.

tricks.label: Bone touches nerve
tricks.text: Picture where a nerve lies directly on bone: axillary around the surgical neck, radial in the spiral groove, ulnar behind the medial epicondyle, common fibular around the fibular neck. The fracture site predicts the nerve.

highYield: Surgical neck fracture of the humerus injures the axillary nerve; midshaft fracture injures the radial nerve.
Pterion fracture tears the middle meningeal artery, causing an epidural hematoma with a lucid interval.
Severe thoracic scoliosis causes restrictive lung disease from reduced chest wall expansion.
Fibular neck fracture causes foot drop from common fibular nerve injury.
Scaphoid fracture risks avascular necrosis of the proximal pole because blood enters distally.
Femoral neck fracture risks avascular necrosis from damage to the medial circumflex femoral artery.
The dens of C2 is the pivot for head rotation.
pitfalls: Anatomical neck fractures of the humerus are rare; the surgical neck is the classic site for axillary nerve injury.
Foramen spinosum carries the middle meningeal artery; foramen ovale carries V3.
Kyphosis is a front to back curve; scoliosis is a side to side curve with rotation.
CN VII enters the internal acoustic meatus but exits the skull through the stylomastoid foramen.

dumps.p: Draw the floor of the skull from above and label the openings from the optic canal back to the foramen magnum. Write what passes through each one.
l: Optic canal: CN II and ophthalmic artery
Superior orbital fissure: CN III, IV, V1, VI
Foramen rotundum: V2
Foramen ovale: V3
Foramen spinosum: middle meningeal artery
Internal acoustic meatus: CN VII and VIII
Jugular foramen: CN IX, X, XI and internal jugular vein
Foramen magnum: medulla and vertebral arteries

dumps.p: Make a table with three columns: fracture site, nerve or vessel at risk, and the deficit you would test. Fill it for the upper and lower limb.
l: Humeral surgical neck: axillary nerve, weak abduction
Midshaft humerus: radial nerve, wrist drop
Supracondylar humerus: median nerve and brachial artery
Medial epicondyle: ulnar nerve, claw hand
Scaphoid: avascular necrosis of proximal pole
Femoral neck: medial circumflex femoral artery, avascular necrosis
Fibular neck: common fibular nerve, foot drop

summary: How joints are classified, how they are innervated, and how the shoulder, knee, and jaw stay stable. Exam questions give a dislocation, a positive exam test, or referred pain and ask which structure is involved.

points: By movement: synarthrosis (immovable), amphiarthrosis (slightly movable), diarthrosis (freely movable, all synovial).
Hinge: humeroulnar joint, interphalangeal joints (flexion and extension).
Pivot: median atlantoaxial joint, proximal radioulnar joint (rotation).
Ball and socket: shoulder, hip (movement in all axes).
Saddle: first carpometacarpal joint (thumb opposition). Condyloid: wrist, metacarpophalangeal joints.
Plane: acromioclavicular and intercarpal joints (gliding).
Hilton law: nerves to the muscles that move a joint also supply that joint and the skin over it.
Joint nerves carry proprioception (position sense) and nociception (pain).
The hip is supplied by the femoral, obturator, and sciatic nerves; the obturator and femoral nerves also supply the knee region.
Hip disease (for example slipped capital femoral epiphysis) can therefore present as knee pain.
Glenoid fossa is shallow, and the labrum only deepens it slightly, so bone gives little stability.
Rotator cuff tendons hold the humeral head in the glenoid (dynamic stability).
Anterior dislocation is most common, usually with the arm abducted and externally rotated.
The axillary nerve wraps the surgical neck and is stretched in anterior dislocation.
Axillary nerve injury: weak abduction past about 15 degrees (deltoid), weak lateral rotation (teres minor), numb skin over the lower deltoid.
ACL runs from the anterior tibia to the lateral femoral condyle and stops forward slide of the tibia.
PCL runs from the posterior tibia to the medial femoral condyle and stops backward slide of the tibia.
MCL resists valgus stress (blow to the outside of the knee); LCL resists varus stress.
Medial meniscus is attached to the MCL and capsule, so it moves less and tears more often.
Classic unhappy triad from a lateral blow: ACL, MCL, and medial meniscus.
Synovial joint between the mandibular condyle and the temporal bone, divided by an articular disc.
Lower compartment allows hinge rotation; upper compartment allows gliding (translation) onto the articular eminence.
Lateral pterygoid pulls the condyle and disc forward to open and protrude the jaw.
Innervated by the auriculotemporal and masseteric branches of CN V3.
Anterior disc displacement: on opening, the condyle snaps forward under the displaced disc and clicks; jaw pain and limited opening can follow.

charts.title: Synovial joint types
rows: Flexion and extension in one plane

tricks.label: Ligament letters
tricks.text: ACL attaches to the Anterior tibia and runs to the Lateral femur. PCL is the opposite: posterior tibia to medial femur. The name tells you where it sits on the tibia.

tricks.label: Valgus pushes the knee in
tricks.text: A valgus force pushes the knee toward the midline and stretches the medial side, so it tests the MCL. Varus stretches the lateral side and tests the LCL.

tricks.label: Knee pain, check the hip
tricks.text: Because of Hilton law, the obturator and femoral nerves carry pain from the hip and the knee region. Always examine the hip in a child or adolescent with knee pain.

highYield: Anterior shoulder dislocation stretches the axillary nerve, causing deltoid weakness and numbness over the lower deltoid.
The rotator cuff provides most glenohumeral stability because the glenoid is shallow.
Lachman test is the most sensitive exam test for an ACL tear.
Medial meniscus tears more often because it is fixed to the MCL.
Hip disease can present as knee pain through the obturator and femoral nerves.
TMJ clicking points to articular disc displacement.
The first carpometacarpal joint is a saddle joint; the median atlantoaxial joint is a pivot.
pitfalls: A positive anterior drawer points to the ACL; a positive posterior drawer points to the PCL.
Valgus stress tests the MCL, even though the force is applied to the lateral knee.
Posterior shoulder dislocation is rare and classically follows seizures or electric shock.
The TMJ disc sits in a synovial joint; TMJ articular surfaces are covered with fibrocartilage.

dumps.p: Draw the top of the tibia viewed from above. Place the medial and lateral menisci, the ACL, the PCL, and the collateral ligaments, then write the clinical test for each.
l: ACL attaches anteriorly on the tibia
PCL attaches posteriorly on the tibia
Medial meniscus is C-shaped and attached to the MCL
Lateral meniscus is more circular and more mobile
Anterior drawer and Lachman test the ACL
Posterior drawer tests the PCL
Valgus stress tests the MCL; varus stress tests the LCL
Unhappy triad: ACL, MCL, medial meniscus

dumps.p: Draw the glenohumeral joint from the front, then draw an anterior dislocation. Trace the axillary nerve and list what the patient loses.
l: Glenoid is shallow; labrum deepens it
Rotator cuff provides dynamic stability
Anterior dislocation is most common
Mechanism is abduction plus external rotation
Axillary nerve wraps the surgical neck of the humerus
Deltoid weakness gives weak abduction
Teres minor weakness gives weak lateral rotation
Numb skin over the lower deltoid

summary: The action and nerve supply of the rotator cuff, the limb muscles, the head and neck muscles, and the trunk muscles. Exam questions give a weakness or a deformity and ask which nerve or muscle is injured.

points: Supraspinatus: starts abduction (first about 15 degrees); suprascapular nerve.
Infraspinatus: lateral rotation; suprascapular nerve.
Teres minor: lateral rotation; axillary nerve.
Subscapularis: medial rotation; upper and lower subscapular nerves.
Supraspinatus is injured most often, from impingement under the acromion; test with the empty can test.
Musculocutaneous: weak elbow flexion and supination (biceps, brachialis), numb lateral forearm.
Radial: wrist drop from paralysis of wrist and finger extensors; high lesions also weaken the triceps.
Median at the wrist: thenar atrophy and loss of thumb opposition (ape hand), numb lateral three and a half fingers (palm spared in carpal tunnel syndrome).
Median at the elbow: also loses lateral finger flexors, so a fist shows the hand of benediction.
Ulnar: claw hand (4th and 5th digits) and weak finger abduction and adduction (interossei).
Long thoracic: serratus anterior paralysis gives a winged scapula; injured in axillary surgery.
Femoral: weak knee extension (quadriceps), lost patellar reflex, numb anterior thigh.
Obturator: weak thigh adduction, numb medial thigh.
Superior gluteal: weak gluteus medius and minimus; standing on the injured leg, the pelvis drops on the opposite side (Trendelenburg sign).
Inferior gluteal: weak gluteus maximus, trouble rising from a chair or climbing stairs.
Common fibular: foot drop, steppage gait, weak eversion, numb dorsum of foot.
Tibial: weak plantarflexion, inversion, and toe flexion; numb sole.
Muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids): CN V3.
Masseter, temporalis, and medial pterygoid close the jaw; lateral pterygoid opens and protrudes it.
Muscles of facial expression: CN VII.
All tongue muscles are CN XII except palatoglossus (CN X); a CN XII lesion makes the tongue deviate toward the injured side.
Sternocleidomastoid (turns the head to the opposite side) and trapezius (shrugs the shoulder): CN XI.
Erector spinae extend the back and are supplied by dorsal rami.
Diaphragm is the main muscle of inspiration; phrenic nerve C3 to C5.
Abdominal wall (external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis, rectus abdominis): thoracoabdominal nerves (T7 to T11), subcostal nerve (T12), and L1 branches.
Levator ani (puborectalis, pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus) forms the pelvic floor and supports pelvic organs; puborectalis helps fecal continence.

charts.title: Limb nerve injuries
rows: Ape hand; hand of benediction if lesion is proximal
Weak knee extension, lost patellar reflex

tricks.label: SItS
tricks.text: Rotator cuff: Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, teres minor, Subscapularis. The small t reminds you teres minor is the one with a different nerve (axillary).

tricks.label: C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive
tricks.text: The phrenic nerve comes from C3 to C5. A spinal cord injury above C3 stops spontaneous breathing.

tricks.label: M's munch, lateral lowers
tricks.text: Masseter, teMporalis, and Medial pterygoid close the jaw (they munch). The Lateral pterygoid Lowers the jaw (opens it).

tricks.label: Trendelenburg: the good side sags
tricks.text: The gluteus medius on the stance leg holds the pelvis level. If it is weak, the pelvis drops on the opposite, lifted side. The lesion is on the side of the leg the patient stands on.

highYield: Supraspinatus is the most commonly injured rotator cuff muscle.
Teres minor is the only rotator cuff muscle supplied by the axillary nerve.
Midshaft humerus fracture or crutch pressure in the axilla gives wrist drop (radial nerve).
Long thoracic nerve injury after mastectomy causes a winged scapula.
Superior gluteal nerve injury gives a positive Trendelenburg sign with drop of the opposite hip.
Common fibular nerve injury gives foot drop and loss of eversion.
Tongue deviates toward the side of a CN XII lesion.
Diaphragm irritation refers pain to the shoulder through C3 to C5.
pitfalls: Supraspinatus starts abduction; the deltoid takes over after about 15 degrees.
Infraspinatus and teres minor both laterally rotate but have different nerves (suprascapular versus axillary).
Ape hand comes from median nerve injury; claw hand comes mainly from ulnar nerve injury.
In Trendelenburg sign the pelvis drops on the side opposite the injured nerve.
Palatoglossus is the one tongue muscle supplied by CN X.

dumps.p: Make a table of the musculocutaneous, radial, median, ulnar, axillary, and long thoracic nerves. For each, list the key muscles, the classic sign of injury, and a common injury site.
l: Musculocutaneous: biceps and brachialis, weak elbow flexion
Radial: extensors, wrist drop, midshaft humerus
Median: thenar muscles, ape hand, carpal tunnel or supracondylar fracture
Ulnar: interossei, claw hand, medial epicondyle
Axillary: deltoid and teres minor, weak abduction, surgical neck or dislocation
Long thoracic: serratus anterior, winged scapula, axillary surgery

dumps.p: Make a table of the femoral, obturator, superior gluteal, inferior gluteal, common fibular, and tibial nerves. For each, list the key muscles, the movement lost, and the sign you would see.
l: Femoral: quadriceps, knee extension, lost patellar reflex
Obturator: adductors, thigh adduction
Superior gluteal: gluteus medius and minimus, Trendelenburg sign
Inferior gluteal: gluteus maximus, trouble climbing stairs
Common fibular: dorsiflexors and evertors, foot drop
Tibial: plantarflexors and tibialis posterior, weak plantarflexion and inversion

summary: Where bone, cartilage, and tendon come from, which collagen types sit in which tissues, how collagen and elastic fibers are built, and why cartilage and tendons heal slowly. Exam questions name a vitamin, mineral, or gene defect and ask which collagen step fails.

points: Limb bones, cartilage, and tendons come from lateral plate (somatic) mesoderm.
Vertebrae and ribs come from sclerotome (paraxial mesoderm).
Most of the face and the pharyngeal arch cartilages come from neural crest mesenchyme.
Skeletal muscle itself comes from somite myotomes, so a limb's muscles and its tendons have different origins.
Type I: bone, tendon, ligament, skin, fibrocartilage (annulus fibrosus); about 90 percent of body collagen.
Type II: hyaline cartilage, nucleus pulposus, vitreous humor.
Type III: reticular fibers, blood vessels, skin, early granulation tissue.
Type IV: basement membrane (network, not fibrils).
Inside the cell (RER): alpha chains are made with repeating Gly-X-Y, where X and Y are often proline and lysine.
Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases add OH groups; they need vitamin C (ascorbate) and iron.
Some hydroxylysines are glycosylated.
Three chains wind into a triple helix (procollagen), lined up by disulfide bonds between their C-terminal propeptides, and are secreted.
Outside the cell: procollagen peptidases cut off the end propeptides to make tropocollagen.
Lysyl oxidase (needs copper) forms covalent cross-links between tropocollagen molecules in the fibril.
Scurvy: no vitamin C, poor hydroxylation, weak triple helix; bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhage, poor wound healing.
Osteogenesis imperfecta: COL1A1 or COL1A2 mutation (often glycine substitution) gives too little or faulty type I collagen; fragile bones, blue sclerae, hearing loss.
Menkes disease: X-linked ATP7A mutation blocks copper transport, so lysyl oxidase cannot cross-link; kinky hair, hypotonia, neurodegeneration.
Aggrecan carries chondroitin and keratan sulfate chains and binds hyaluronan through link protein.
These negative GAGs pull in cations and water, which pushes back against compression; type II collagen resists stretch.
Articular cartilage has no blood vessels, so chondrocytes get nutrients by diffusion and repair is poor.
Tendons have few cells and a poor blood supply, so they heal slowly.
Elastic fibers have an elastin core laid on fibrillin-1 microfibrils; elastin is cross-linked by desmosine.
Elastic fibers fill the ligamentum flavum (yellow ligament), which recoils when the spine straightens.
Fibrillin-1 binds latent TGF-beta; in Marfan syndrome (FBN1 mutation) TGF-beta is released and overactive.

tricks.label: Be So Totally Cool, Read Books
tricks.text: Type I: Bone, Skin, Tendon. Type II: Cartilage. Type III: Reticulin. Type IV: Basement membrane.

tricks.label: Type II: cartwolage
tricks.text: Type II collagen is in cartilage, including the nucleus pulposus and vitreous body.

tricks.label: C for collagen, Cu for cross-links
tricks.text: Vitamin C works inside the cell (hydroxylation). Copper works outside the cell (lysyl oxidase cross-links). Scurvy breaks the inside step; Menkes breaks the outside step.

highYield: Vitamin C is a cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase; deficiency weakens the triple helix.
Lysyl oxidase needs copper; Menkes disease (ATP7A) blocks cross-linking.
Osteogenesis imperfecta is most often a type I collagen defect (COL1A1 or COL1A2).
Hyaline cartilage and nucleus pulposus are type II collagen; annulus fibrosus is type I.
Aggrecan GAGs hold water, which lets articular cartilage resist compression.
Fibrillin-1 sequesters TGF-beta; FBN1 mutation in Marfan syndrome raises TGF-beta signaling.
Ligamentum flavum is rich in elastic fibers.
pitfalls: Hydroxylation happens inside the cell; cross-linking happens outside the cell.
Type IV collagen forms sheets in basement membranes, not fibrils.
Limb tendons come from lateral plate mesoderm even though limb muscles come from somites.
Fibrillin-1 is the scaffold that is defective in Marfan syndrome; elastin is the stretchy core laid on it. Lysyl oxidase cross-links both collagen and elastin (desmosine).

dumps.p: Draw a fibroblast and trace collagen synthesis from the RER to a cross-linked fibril outside the cell. At each step, write what it needs and the disease when it fails.
l: Alpha chains are made in the RER with Gly-X-Y repeats
Proline and lysine hydroxylation needs vitamin C and iron (scurvy)
Hydroxylysine glycosylation
Triple helix forms as procollagen
Procollagen is secreted
Peptidases cleave propeptides to form tropocollagen
Lysyl oxidase with copper cross-links fibrils (Menkes)
Faulty or reduced type I chains cause osteogenesis imperfecta

dumps.p: Draw a piece of articular cartilage matrix showing hyaluronan, aggrecan, GAG chains, and type II collagen. Explain how it resists compression and why it heals poorly.
l: Hyaluronan backbone
Aggrecan core proteins attached through link protein
Chondroitin sulfate and keratan sulfate chains are negatively charged
Negative charges draw in cations and water
Bound water resists compression
Type II collagen network resists tension
No blood vessels, so nutrients arrive by diffusion and repair is slow

summary: How skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle turn an electrical or chemical signal into force, and how force is graded. Exam questions give a channel, drug, or training change and ask how contraction or relaxation will change.

points: An action potential spreads along the sarcolemma and down the T tubules.
The dihydropyridine receptor (L-type voltage sensor) in the T tubule changes shape.
It is mechanically linked to ryanodine receptor 1 (RyR1) on the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which opens and releases calcium.
Skeletal muscle does not need calcium entry from outside the cell to contract.
Calcium binds troponin C, which moves tropomyosin off the myosin binding sites on actin.
SERCA pumps calcium back into the SR (uses ATP), and the muscle relaxes.
Starting point: myosin head tightly bound to actin with no nucleotide (rigor state).
ATP binds myosin and releases it from actin.
ATP hydrolysis cocks the head; ADP and phosphate stay bound.
Head binds actin; phosphate release drives the power stroke; then ADP leaves.
Rigor mortis: without ATP, myosin cannot detach from actin, so muscles lock a few hours after death.
A motor unit is one motor neuron plus all the fibers it supplies.
Size principle: small motor units (slow, type I) are recruited first and large ones (fast, type II) last.
Summation: a second action potential before relaxation adds force, because the twitch lasts longer than the action potential.
At high firing rates twitches fuse into tetanus, the maximal sustained force.
Length-tension: active force is greatest at the resting sarcomere length with optimal actin-myosin overlap; too stretched or too short lowers force.
Force-velocity: the heavier the load, the slower the shortening; velocity is maximal at zero load and zero at maximal (isometric) force.
During the plateau, calcium enters through L-type calcium channels.
This calcium triggers RyR2 to release more calcium from the SR (calcium-induced calcium release).
The long refractory period lasts nearly as long as contraction, so cardiac muscle cannot summate or go into tetany.
Sympathetic beta-1 stimulation raises cAMP and activates protein kinase A.
PKA phosphorylates L-type channels (more calcium entry) and phospholamban.
Phosphorylated phospholamban stops inhibiting SERCA2, so the SR refills faster: faster relaxation and stronger next beat.
Calcium enters through L-type channels or is released from the SR through IP3 receptors.
Calcium binds calmodulin; calcium-calmodulin activates myosin light chain kinase (MLCK).
MLCK phosphorylates the myosin light chain, which turns on cross-bridge cycling; smooth muscle has no troponin.
Myosin light chain phosphatase removes the phosphate and causes relaxation.
Latch state: dephosphorylated myosin stays attached and cycles slowly, holding tone with little ATP.
Nitric oxide activates guanylyl cyclase; cGMP activates protein kinase G, lowers calcium, and activates the phosphatase, causing relaxation.
Type I: slow, oxidative, red (myoglobin), many mitochondria and capillaries, fatigue resistant; posture muscles such as soleus.
Type II: fast, glycolytic, white, large glycogen stores, high force, fatigable.
Endurance training raises mitochondria, capillaries, and oxidative enzymes.
Resistance training enlarges type II fibers by adding myofibrils (hypertrophy).

charts.title: Cross-bridge cycle
rows: Head cocks with ADP and phosphate bound
Power stroke pulls actin toward the M line
Rigor state until new ATP binds

tricks.label: One slow red ox
tricks.text: Type 1 fibers are slow twitch, red, and use oxidative phosphorylation.

tricks.label: ATP lets go
tricks.text: ATP is needed to release myosin from actin and to pump calcium back into the SR. With no ATP, muscle cannot relax, which is rigor mortis.

tricks.label: Smooth muscle switch is on myosin
tricks.text: Skeletal and cardiac muscle regulate the thin filament (troponin and tropomyosin). Smooth muscle regulates the thick filament (phosphorylating the myosin light chain).

highYield: Skeletal DHPR is mechanically coupled to RyR1; cardiac contraction depends on calcium entry triggering RyR2.
RyR1 mutation causes malignant hyperthermia with volatile anesthetics; dantrolene blocks RyR1.
ATP binding detaches myosin from actin; loss of ATP causes rigor mortis.
Small motor units are recruited first (size principle).
Phospholamban phosphorylation by PKA speeds SERCA2, improving relaxation and contractility.
The long cardiac refractory period prevents tetany.
Nitric oxide relaxes smooth muscle through cGMP; PDE5 inhibitors prolong this effect.
Endurance training raises oxidative capacity; resistance training enlarges type II fibers.
pitfalls: The power stroke happens with phosphate release; ATP binding causes detachment.
Smooth muscle uses calmodulin; skeletal and cardiac muscle use troponin C.
Phosphorylating the myosin light chain contracts smooth muscle; the phosphatase relaxes it.
Tetanus in muscle physiology means fused maximal contraction from rapid firing; the disease tetanus is caused by Clostridium tetani toxin.
Phospholamban inhibits SERCA when unphosphorylated; PKA phosphorylation removes that brake.

dumps.p: Draw a T tubule next to the SR for a skeletal fiber and for a cardiac cell. Show how calcium is released in each, how it is removed, and why only one can go into tetany.
l: Action potential travels down the T tubule
Skeletal: DHPR mechanically opens RyR1
Cardiac: L-type calcium entry triggers RyR2 (calcium-induced calcium release)
Calcium binds troponin C and moves tropomyosin
SERCA returns calcium to the SR
Phospholamban regulates SERCA2 in the heart; PKA phosphorylation speeds it
Cardiac long refractory period prevents tetany
Skeletal summation and tetanus come from rapid firing

dumps.p: Draw a smooth muscle cell and trace the pathway from a rise in calcium to contraction, then from nitric oxide to relaxation.
l: Calcium enters through L-type channels or SR IP3 receptors
Calcium binds calmodulin
Calcium-calmodulin activates MLCK
MLCK phosphorylates the myosin light chain and starts cross-bridge cycling
Myosin light chain phosphatase dephosphorylates and relaxes
Latch state holds tone with little ATP
Nitric oxide activates guanylyl cyclase and raises cGMP
Protein kinase G lowers calcium and activates the phosphatase
